title: 5 storylines to watch as Falcons open training camp under Kevin Stefanski Quarterback is the chief question as the Falcons head into training camp, but it's not the only one. Josh Kendall

full_text:
Michael Penix Jr. will be in the spotlight as he and Tua Tagovailoa compete for the Falcons' starting job. Todd Kirkland / Getty Images
The Atlanta Falcons’ veterans report to training camp on Tuesday, joining the rookies who reported on Friday, and the full team’s first day on the practice field is Wednesday. That means we’ll finally start getting some answers about what new coach Kevin Stefanski’s team will look like.
Here are the top five storylines heading into camp, starting, of course, at quarterback.
The first question is whether Michael Penix Jr. will be cleared for full work. He was held out of 11-on-11 drills throughout the spring while rehabbing the torn ACL he suffered on Nov. 16. He did work in seven-on-seven drills and expressed optimism that he would be a full participant for the opening day of training camp, but Stefanski stopped short of predicting that.
Penix, who enters his third year in the league after being the eighth pick in the 2024 draft, is fighting with six-year veteran Tua Tagovailoa to retain the starting job Penix held before his injury last year. Tagovailoa joined the Falcons on a one-year, $1.2 million contract after being released by the Dolphins.
The competition “has been nothing but good since he got here,” Penix said. “We know we’re in a competition, but we’re on the same team and have the same goals, and that’s to win games. We’ve been good together.”
The Falcons have had five players start at quarterback (Desmond Ridder, Marcus Mariota, Taylor Heinicke, Kirk Cousins and Penix) since trading Matt Ryan following the 2021 season. Ryan, Falcons fans no doubt remember, was hired in the offseason as Atlanta’s new president of football.
The Falcons’ second-year edge rusher is expected to participate in training camp despite his ongoing legal situation. Pearce, who was arrested in February and faces three felony charges in Florida following a domestic dispute with former girlfriend Rickea Jackson, skipped all of the team’s voluntary workouts during the offseason but was on the field for a two-day minicamp in June. He is enrolled in a 12-month pretrial intervention program that could result in all of his charges being dismissed, but the NFL is still expected to impose a suspension.
The league has wide latitude to suspend players under its personal-conduct policy regardless of the outcome of criminal proceedings, and situations similar to Pearce’s have resulted in multiple-game suspensions. Pearce finished third in Defensive Rookie of the Year voting last year after leading all first-year players — and the Falcons — with 10.5 sacks.
“We’ll see if we’ve got a guy here who can replace that role,” defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich said this spring. “I’m excited about the guys that we have, whether it be Samson (Ebukam) or Bralen (Trice). There are countless guys, like Azeez (Ojulari), and we’ll see what they can do collectively.”
For the second straight year, Atlanta is making a change at right tackle. Kaleb McGary, who was the 31st pick in the 2019 draft and started 92 games at right tackle from 2019 to 2024, retired in the offseason after missing all of the 2025 season due to a knee injury. Last year, the Falcons filled in with Elijah Wilkinson, who left in free agency this offseason.
Now Atlanta is going with Jawaan Taylor, who was picked four spots after McGary in the 2019 draft. Taylor has started 120 games for the Jaguars and Chiefs over the last seven years, including nine in the playoffs. He signed a one-year, $5 million deal shortly after McGary retired in April, but he sat out the spring with a leg injury. He is expected to be ready for training camp.
Two months after adding Taylor, the Falcons traded for Wanya Morris, who was Taylor’s backup in Kansas City for the last three seasons. Morris was a third-round pick in 2023.
The nine wide receivers on Atlanta’s roster who aren’t Drake London have a total of 317 catches in 16 NFL seasons. Most of those come from free-agent additions Olamide Zaccheaus (188 catches in seven years) and Jahan Dotson (121 in four years). That looks like the Falcons’ three-man starting lineup to start the season, at least.
Third-round draft pick Zachariah Branch will be in that rotation and could bump Dotson or Zaccheaus from the starting lineup if he has a strong training camp. After that, Chris Blair (one catch in three seasons) and Dylan Drummond (seven catches in two seasons) are next in line simply because they’ve seen an NFL field. UDFAs Vinny Anthony II, Keelan Marion, Le’Meke Brockington and free agent Antwane Wells Jr. fill out the roster heading into camp, but general manager Ian Cunningham will be scouring the league for the next five weeks in hopes of strengthening that room.
The first few days of training camp will give us a better idea of who’s healthy and who’s not. Several players — such as Taylor, safety Xavier Watts and fourth-round linebacker Kendal Daniels — sat out the spring with what Stefanski characterized as minor injuries. All three are expected back on the field at full speed this week, and it will be notable if they’re not.
Of more interest will be players such as cornerback Billy Bowman and linebackers JD Bertrand and Troy Andersen. Bowman suffered a torn Achilles in November and was held out throughout the spring. Bertrand and Andersen were also sidelined this spring, and both are entering a critical training camp. Bertrand, a fifth-round pick in 2024 who started two games last year, could have a hard time making the 53-man roster after the Falcons added four linebackers in the offseason.
Andersen would be expected to make the roster if he were healthy, but he hasn’t been healthy in a long time. A second-round pick in 2022, he hasn’t played since Week 14 of the 2024 season. He has started 11 games in three years while missing time due to a concussion, a torn pectoral muscle and multiple knee issues.

full_text:
An offseason of change brings yet another intriguing season in Orchard Park as the Buffalo Bills kick off training camp practices Wednesday. Nic Antaya / Getty Images
After a long wait and, at times, a topsy-turvy offseason, the Buffalo Bills are officially back in action on Wednesday.
The team conducts its first training camp practice of 2026 at St. John Fisher University with several questions to answer after an offseason of significant changes. A new head coach, a new defense and defensive coordinator, and a pretty major roster refresh on that side of the ball to go with it.
Those answers will all come over the next several weeks, as general manager Brandon Beane needs to make some difficult decisions ahead of final cuts. Some years have been easier than others for final cuts, but this year’s group has several decision points currently up in the air.
How could it all shake out at several key spots?
Here is our Bills 53-man roster projection to jumpstart training camp and the official beginning of the 2026 season.
After bringing back Mitchell Trubisky for the last two seasons and having one of the league’s better backup situations, the Bills now have one of the bigger dropoffs from starter to backup in 2026. Kyle Allen and Josh Allen share a close relationship — and that’s something the team values in constructing the quarterback room. The Bills had to choose low-cost options in some areas of the roster, and in this case, they do so at backup quarterback behind a starter who hasn’t missed a game since 2018.
James Cook, Ray Davis, Ty Johnson, Jackson Acker (FB)
It appears the Bills will go with the trio of Cook, Davis and Johnson for a third straight season. Whether their roles are as defined under Joe Brady as head coach as they were in the last two seasons remains to be seen. The Bills likely will have a new fullback on the 53-man roster this season, filling the role vacated by Reggie Gilliam. I gave the edge to Acker, the undrafted rookie out of Wisconsin, because he has the advantage of being on a three-year deal, is a restricted free agent after that and has more guaranteed money than the veteran free-agent pickup Ben VanSumeren.
Cut: Frank Gore Jr., Ian Wheeler, Ben VanSumeren (FB)
DJ Moore, Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman, Joshua Palmer, Skyler Bell
The Bills have a few interesting names who could push for the 53-man roster, but with so many spots needed for their offensive line investments and a new defensive scheme, picking five to make the initial roster seems like the most efficient use of assets at this point. Palmer could be one to monitor, but his versatility within the scheme and knowledge of it make him far more likely to make it than not. Hardman is one to monitor for his punt-returning skills, though he would need to vastly outshine other options for a onesie role. Hardman is also hurt by rookie Skyler Bell having a real chance to earn the same role, and by the fact that Bell is a mid-round pick the team is high on. At some point later in the season, they could get Tyrell Shavers back from his torn ACL, which would be a good way to keep six receivers while initially having only five.
Physically Unable to Perform (PUP): Tyrell Shavers Cut: Mecole Hardman, Trent Sherfield, Jalen Virgil, Stephen Gosnell, Ja’Mori Maclin, Mac Delena, Max Tomczak, Quentin Skinner
Dalton Kincaid, Dawson Knox, Jackson Hawes
With Knox agreeing to a new contract this offseason, the Bills likely keep the same tight end room from 2025. Knox is the balance between the receiving and running games. Kincaid is the top receiving threat in the trio, with the team hoping his role increases from last season. Hawes is the bruising blocker with a better receiving profile than he gets credit for. Rather than who makes the team, the real question under Brady as head coach is how — and how often — they’re deployed.
Cut: Keleki Latu, Shane Zylstra
Dion Dawkins, Connor McGovern, O’Cyrus Torrence, Spencer Brown, Alec Anderson, Austin Corbett, Jude Bowry, Lloyd Cushenberry III, Tylan Grable, Sedrick Van Pran-Granger
Without question, there is a tough decision or two coming from this offensive line group. They have a healthy mix of draft investments and veteran options along their reserve group, putting them in an uncomfortable spot with 11 legitimate rosterable options by the start of the regular season. The Bills generally prefer to keep at most 10 offensive linemen under Beane, setting up a major decision this summer. I think the group it could come down to is between Cushenberry, Grable, Van Pran-Granger, and Chase Lundt.
With it comes an opportunity that Beane generally takes advantage of ahead of final cuts — shipping out a reserve offensive lineman for draft compensation rather than cutting one for nothing. With this year’s group, I landed on Lundt. Although they just drafted Lundt in 2025, things have changed at offensive tackle. The team drafted Bowry in the early fourth round this year, while Grable — who can play tackle or guard — has more positional flexibility than Lundt. Lundt is mostly a right tackle-only prospect. They could look to trade Grable or Van Pran-Granger as well, but as of now, Lundt seems like the most logical candidate.
Traded before final cuts: Chase Lundt Cut: Ar’maj Reed-Adams, Nick Broeker, Bruno Fina, De’Metrius Weatherspoon, Travis Clayton
Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, T.J. Sanders, Landon Jackson, DeWayne Carter, Zane Durant
The defensive line group is tough to gauge because it has a lot of unknowns. Sanders is transitioning to a new position and could be expected to start. Jackson is coming off a season-ending injury, packed on a bunch of weight and is switching to a new role in a new defense. Carter is making his comeback from a season-ending ruptured Achilles, and whether he can be a rotational nose tackle for them remains to be seen. It could make the case a bit stronger for keeping someone like Phidarian Mathis, who can play a few roles in their defense. However, with very little guaranteed money in his deal, Mathis could be more of a practice-squad type who eventually works his way onto the active roster as injuries occur during the year.
Cut: Phidarian Mathis, Tommy Akingbesote, Zion Logue, Kody Huisman
Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, T.J. Parker, Michael Hoecht, Mike Danna, Javon Solomon
The Bills made three noteworthy additions to this group during the offseason: Chubb, Parker and Danna, and Danna’s guaranteed money ($1.26 million) makes him a good bet to make the team. The big question is about Hoecht and his timeline to return to play (torn right Achilles tendon). Things have been trending positively throughout the spring, but Hoecht taking a roster spot to begin the year could weaken the Bills elsewhere. Solomon could be on the roster bubble because of how many outside linebackers are ahead of him, though his special teams abilities make him safe for now.
Cut: Andre Jones Jr., Cade Denhoff
Terrel Bernard, Dorian Williams, Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Joe Andreessen
This inside linebacker group has three definites in Bernard, Williams and Elarms-Orr and one near-lock in Andreessen for his special-teams abilities. It remains to be seen if it will be Williams or Elarms-Orr starting next to Bernard to begin the year, or if they work all three into the lineup. The intrigue with this group is high, considering the investments in Bernard and Elarms-Orr, and with Williams in the final year of his rookie deal.
Cut: Keonta Jenkins, Jimmy Ciarlo, Theron Gaines, Demetrius Flannigan-Fowles
Dee Alford, Jordan Hancock
Although the Bills haven’t dedicated Hancock to a position at this point, the logical choice is for him to be the primary backup to Alford at nickel. The Bills have plenty of safeties on their roster they added in the offseason and are light at nickel if Hancock wasn’t a part of the group.
Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston, Davison Igbinosun
Three at this position seems light, but it’s fair to note a couple of things. The first: Do not be surprised…

title: Lions training camp preview: They have work ahead — and Dan Campbell is ready for it Will the offense elevate with a new offensive coordinator? What will DC Kelvin Sheppard do to keep the defense on track? Colton Pouncy 4
summary: Lions training camp preview: They have work ahead — and Dan Campbell is ready for it Will the offense elevate with a new offensive coordinator? What will DC Kelvin Sheppard do to keep the defense on track? Colton Pouncy
full_text:
Will Isaac Teslaa and the rest of the Detroit offense return to form in Drew Petzing's first season as offensive coordinator? Gregory Shamus / Getty Images
By this time Wednesday, the Detroit Lions will take the field for the start of training camp, and what they hope will be a return to form after a disappointing 2025 season.
It’s a pivotal year for coach Dan Campbell and company, who’ve quietly gone about their business this offseason. They had a meat-and-potatoes free agency and draft, emphasizing depth and positions of need. Don’t expect to hear this group openly talk about the playoffs, Super Bowl or anything beyond the immediate. That’s not where their focus is. They have to earn the right to have those convos again.
Right now, it’s all about the work — and that work begins Wednesday.
If you’ve been following along this offseason, you might’ve heard some of the changes Campbell plans to make in training camp that differ from previous seasons. If not, allow us to catch you up to speed.
• Campbell said he expects this to be the most competitive training camp the Lions have had since he’s been here. That was a goal for him and GM Brad Holmes, and it’s reflective of their offseason additions. Campbell wants to get back to the early days of his tenure, when competition got the best out of his players.
• Campbell said the Lions will “be smart” about getting his players ready for the 2026 season. He said, “We’re going to push it. We’re going to push, that’s what we do, but we’ll do it smart. We have got to get these guys ready for a season. … I’m going to do what I think is best to prepare these guys for 17 weeks, but also understand that we have got to be smart about it and we can’t break them in training camp.”
• The Lions will not conduct joint practices for the first time since 2021.
• Campbell said the Lions could play starters in the preseason.
It’ll be interesting to see what other changes come about. But that’s a good baseline of what to expect, as Campbell looks to evolve without getting away from what got him here.
Campbell’s lengthy OC search this offseason after moving on from John Morton led him to Drew Petzing — a man who wasn’t on many radars. He’d spent the last three seasons overseeing an average Cardinals offense. The head coach who hired him, Jonathan Gannon, was fired. It wasn’t a flashy choice. But is it the right one? Campbell believes it is.
Petzing is a teacher. People you talk to about him say he can coach the veteran quarterback down to the late-round rookie from a small school. He can make complicated terminology and concepts digestible — no matter your experience level. Beyond that, though, he’s a coach who looks to exploit weakness, isn’t afraid to zag when others zig and will bring variety to the run game. In Detroit, he’ll have weapons he’s never had at his disposal. We saw a glimpse of the eye-candy motions in OTAs, and should see more of it in training camp. Between Petzing and an improved offensive line, the offense has a chance to return to form in 2026.
The Lions’ defense is under construction. Multiyear starters Alex Anzalone, DJ Reader and Amik Robertson are no longer here. Former first-round pick Terrion Arnold was released in June. Detroit’s starting safeties are both managing serious injuries and won’t be ready for the start of camp. All that to say, there are a lot of moving parts here. That alone presents challenges for Lions second-year DC Kelvin Sheppard.
When this defense was relatively healthy last season, it was starting to look like a top-10 unit. But will the injury bug be too much to overcome again? Can Sheppard navigate the lack of continuity in 2026 with a year of experience under his belt? How will the new pieces fit? Will Sheppard’s offseason deep dive of the defense with Campbell lead to better results? Or will this season look similar to 2022 and 2023 — when the offense had to carry a defense that didn’t have the juice? The season will yield those answers, but training camp will be the first look.
CB2: After the release of Arnold, the Lions have questions at cornerback. D.J. Reed is back for Year 2 of his three-year, $48 million contract, and the hope is that a healthy season leads to more consistency. The Lions need him to play like a CB1. Then we have the CB2 job, one that could come down to Rock Ya-Sin vs. Ennis Rakestraw Jr. Ya-Sin is the early favorite. He filled in admirably for Arnold and Reed when they missed time last season, and the Lions brought him back on a one-year contract for the depth he provides. Will he offer the same caliber of play in a full-time starting role? Or is it time for Rakestraw, a 2024 second-round pick, to win the job?
RT: The Lions seem higher than most on veteran tackle Larry Borom, and believe he’s coming off one of his better seasons manning right tackle for the Dolphins. That said, you have to think the Lions would love nothing more than for their first-round pick, Blake Miller, to win the job. That the Lions drafted Miller in the first round — over prospects like Monroe Freeling and Max Iheanachor — speaks to them favoring a more NFL-ready tackle. Miller started 54 games in four seasons at Clemson and has a strong work ethic. He fits the profile of a tackle who can step in and provide serviceable play at right tackle, even if there are growing pains along the way.
LG: The early sense is this is Christian Mahogany’s job to lose, but the fact the job is in question in ways it wasn’t last year speaks to the improved depth at guard. Mahogany struggled in pass protection and missed time with injury in his first season as a full-time starter. There’s hope he can improve with better health, natural growth and playing between Cade Mays and Penei Sewell. If not, the Lions can turn to Ben Bartch and Miles Frazier. Those are the three names to watch here.
LB: The Lions let Anzalone walk in free agency and need to find a new starting linebacker. The Lions will likely turn first to Malcolm Rodriguez. Back on a one-year deal, Rodriguez fits the run well and has a natural feel for the ball carrier. He leaves a bit to be desired in pass coverage, but the Lions can make up for that by playing more nickel. If this ends up becoming a battle, it’ll be because 2026 fourth-round pick Jimmy Rolder made it one. While he lacks experience, Rolder’s instincts and size could make him an intriguing option if he continues to impress like he did in OTAs.
Safety: The Lions will be without Kerby Joseph (knee) and Brian Branch (Achilles) when training camp begins, with both placed on the PUP list. Not entirely surprising news, but it will give us a look at the next men up. Based on OTAs and minicamp, it seems like Chuck Clark and Christian Izien, a pair of free-agent additions, will get first crack at it. Clark made plays in OTAs, picking off Jared Goff in one of the highlights of June practices, and Izien is a physical, versatile DB the Lions know well from their battles with the Bucs. We’ll see if Avonte Maddox or Thomas Harper can push for starting reps.
As you can tell, the Lions have work to do. Show me a team that doesn’t, though. This is training camp — the time to work out kinks and prepare yourself to have the best possible season. In many ways, the Lions are set up for a bounce-back.
They’ve addressed the majority of their needs head-on, return one of the league’s most talented rosters and have a favorable schedule that sets up for early success. But making the playoffs isn’t the primary goal. Whether or not the Lions have what it takes to win a championship will be settled long after training camp, but this period should offer a good first look as we evaluate this team and how far it can go.

full_text:
A bulky brace on his left leg is just one of the elements Patrick Mahomes is dealing with after knee surgery in December. Jamie Squire / Getty Images
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. — Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes participated in two rookie-centered, closed-to-the-public training camp practices over the weekend before getting a scheduled day off Monday.
Here are three quick observations from watching Mahomes, who has been fully cleared to participate in drills after having surgery to repair the ACL and LCL in his left knee last December.
The Chiefs didn’t appear to waste any time pushing the 30-year-old quarterback.
During Sunday’s practice, Mahomes was part of a group that worked on rollouts to his left. That throwing movement — while done under the close watch of coach Andy Reid — certainly was designed to put at least some early stress on Mahomes’ surgically repaired left knee.
Yes, Mahomes still appeared to be favoring that leg a bit. With it being just seven months since he underwent surgery in Dallas, that should be expected.
The action, nonetheless, told us something about how Mahomes and the Chiefs are approaching his recovery. They will be monitoring him closely, but they also seem eager to test his limits.
Mahomes said Friday that he felt comfortable playing with a knee brace after using one during part of his college career at Texas Tech.
This much became clear in two practices, though: He still will need time to get used to this particular support around his left knee.
While recording videos of Mahomes, I was struck by how many times he reached over to adjust the bulky brace. Sometimes, it would be a quick adjustment. Other times, he’d mess with multiple straps, pulling and tugging until he got them into a better position.
In other words, Mahomes will be dealing with more than physical limitations when he first takes the field this year. He’ll also have to work around a leg harness that isn’t quite comfortable — at least not yet.
This is my fifth training camp covering the Chiefs, and one thing that has stood out so far is that Mahomes appears to be getting a lot more under-center reps.
The Chiefs have typically been a shotgun-heavy team, but that ratio could shift this summer following not only the addition of running back Kenneth Walker III but also after general manager Brett Veach hinted that the team would look to rely more on a downhill run game .
In any case, Mahomes has taken pre-stretch snaps under center and also had seven-on-seven passes begin with that same setup.
While it remains very early — the Chiefs’ first full-squad practice is set for Wednesday — it’ll be worth watching to see if this trend continues throughout the rest of camp.

full_text:
Matthew Stafford returned to the practice field on Monday after missing all of training camp last year to manage a degenerative back issue. Wally Skalij / Associated Press
LOS ANGELES — The Los Angeles Rams are two training camp practices into a journey they hope can carry them all the way to a final game at SoFi Stadium in February.
The work starts on the grass fields at Loyola Marymount University. Here are eight thoughts on what we’ve seen through the first two sessions:
1. This was Matthew Stafford’s first time throwing passes in a training camp setting in two years. A year after he missed it all to manage a degenerative back issue that threatened the start of the season, it feels like he and the passing game are now in a different place. The back issue hasn’t gone anywhere, and he’ll still miss every other practice to manage it. But there’s no longer the threat, the wonder or the fear.
That was on display Monday, when Stafford threw at will to Davante Adams on crossers and deep dig routes that showcased great timing and spatial awareness, and when he let it rip downfield to Puka Nacua. It took them just a couple snaps to create the highlight of the practice, as Nacua went deep down the left sideline on a fade route and Stafford lofted it for a smooth catch-and-run touchdown that got the crowd roaring.
Nacua came back shortly after that on a slant route across the middle. Stafford had to adjust the ball to fit it into a tight window, and Nacua reached up one hand to reel it in without breaking stride before taking it to the house.
Adams isn’t new anymore, Stafford isn’t fearing if he can play and Nacua is simply Nacua. It’s arguably the highest-ceiling foundation any unit in the NFL has, and it’s the reason the Rams were willing to get as aggressive as they’ve been on defense to maximize this group.
2. If Nacua has been the biggest and flashiest star through two practices, the most under-the-radar star has been the newest receiver on the team.
CJ Daniels turned in a terrific practice on Monday as he worked primarily with Stetson Bennett and the second-team offense. The sixth-round rookie out of Miami was Bennett’s go-to option and caught everything that came his way. It’s early, but he’s starting to show glimpses of why the Rams traded up to take him. He’s strong, tough, competitive and confident as both a run blocker and a receiver in traffic. The confidence he attacks the ball at the catch point with is something Sean McVay has long looked for in a receiver.
But Daniels is not a burner, and I do wonder how he’ll look in more difficult matchups than against the second-team defense. But that’s where the role should insulate him well as a rookie. Nacua and Adams will draw the top outside cornerbacks, and teams don’t often have three coverage players with a mix of size and speed. Daniels could find matchups where his 6-foot-2 size is enough of an advantage to mitigate the lack of speed.
It’s interesting to look across the Rams’ skill positions and see the lack of a true burner with Tutu Atwell gone. In fact, the only player who might truly run away from packs of defenders this year is running back Blake Corum. And yet that’s still the model the Rams carried to the No. 1 scoring offense last season, because that’s just what elite balance can do in a scheme like this.
3. The offense does have one new and important element to it, and that’s a new coordinator. Mike LaFleur’s departure to the Arizona Cardinals cleared a lane for Nathan Scheelhaase to get a promotion from passing game coordinator, and it could be a short stint for him as one of the hot head-coaching candidates entering next year’s cycle.
Scheelhaase is walking into a great infrastructure. He has McVay’s system and oversight. He has balance in the offense and versatility in the personnel. He has an MVP quarterback and two star receivers.
But perhaps what helps a 35-year-old first-time coordinator most is that he has essentially two coaches on the field in Stafford and Adams. The Stafford piece goes without explanation, but perhaps equally as important is Adams because, unlike Stafford, he’s not on a pitch count and maintenance schedule. He’s the consistent rock right now.
“He’s a guy that, second to none, cares about his craft and what it looks like to be the best receiver he possibly can be,” Scheelhaase said of Adams. “And you just see over the course of years why he’s been successful. Him coming out here on the first day of a training camp in 10-plus seasons in the league, he’s got the same mentality. He’s trying to figure out small ways to get better, things he can do with his releases, things he can do at the top of his breaks. That’s the type of guy you love being around as a coach.”
4. It helps explain why the Rams ultimately did not pull the trigger on trading Adams for A.J. Brown this offseason. The idea was tantalizing, as Brown is the better player at this stage of their respective careers and could offer a cost-controlled No. 1 receiver in the event that the Rams don’t extend Nacua. But as they constantly preach right now, names on paper don’t win football games. It would have been messing with something that is far from broken — and the biggest effects might be in the steady, even-keeled way Adams has taken to a veteran No. 2 role.
His story will be a fascinating one to document this season. He can feel the end closing in, but it’s the most unresolved of anyone’s story here. Adams is 0-5 in conference championship games. And so while every player hungers to hoist a Lombardi Trophy, Adams has a little more on the line with his attempt to win one. If he does so and is a major piece, that could be the final argument for the Hall of Fame.
“I’ve given it some thought,” Adams said on retirement. “It wasn’t until the past couple of years where, for different reasons, that you start to think about when the end is going to come. Right now, I’m just enjoying it. I can’t tell you if it’s going to be after this year or after next year. I truly don’t know.”
5. Nacua did have one fade route he couldn’t win because Trent McDuffie was in good position. The two-time All-Pro cornerback matched him stride-for-stride and beat him to a Stafford deep pass to knock it away.
McDuffie will be at his best this season moving across a secondary that will try to live in dime personnel as often as possible. He’s most effective in the slot due to his mix of toughness, tackling, communication and instincts. But reps like that against the NFL’s reigning leader in receptions showcase why he’s such a critical addition. The Rams simply didn’t have anyone who could reliably do it from an outside cornerback spot last season, and it froze the creative juices they wanted to deploy in the playoffs.
6. The most impressive play in Sunday’s practice was the diving interception Kam Kinchens made along the sideline off a tipped pass from Cam Lampkin. The ability to see the ball off the ricochet, track it into his arms while falling and stay inbounds shows why I had Kinchens as one of the Rams’ three biggest breakout candidates .
Last season, Kinchens was left trying to play eraser at free safety with the mistakes in run defense and the coverage of the outside cornerbacks. That cut into his playing time, as the Rams had to lean on veterans like Quentin Lake and Kam Curl more, which also spoiled a bit of their own versatility and playmaking. Kinchens isn’t the kind of athlete who’s going to cover for someone else as well, but he can be impactful in making plays on the ball, as his four interceptions, forced fumble, fumble recovery and defensive touchdown as a rookie proved.
7. Stafford’s maintenance schedule is going to serve two purposes. The obvious is to keep him fresh and ready for Week 1 in Melbourne against the San Francisco 49ers. The second is to open up reps for one of the Rams’ only position battles in camp — the backup spot behind him.
With Jimmy Garoppolo gone, that’s fallen on Bennett and No. 13 overall…

title: Pre-training camp NFL Power Rankings: Rams on top, so where are the rival Seahawks? Josh Kendall 15
summary:
Myles Garrett's arrival in Los Angeles makes the Rams our Super Bowl favorites entering the season. Keith Birmingham / MediaNews Group / Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images
The NFL Power Rankings would like to offer a sincere thank you to the World Cup for a fun summer diversion. But our football is back now, and we’re pretty excited.
Training camps are open across the NFL, and the Hall of Fame Game kicks off next week, so we’re checking in on what’s new for all 32 teams and looking at how they
full_text:
Myles Garrett's arrival in Los Angeles makes the Rams our Super Bowl favorites entering the season. Keith Birmingham / MediaNews Group / Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images
The NFL Power Rankings would like to offer a sincere thank you to the World Cup for a fun summer diversion. But our football is back now, and we’re pretty excited.
Training camps are open across the NFL, and the Hall of Fame Game kicks off next week, so we’re checking in on what’s new for all 32 teams and looking at how they stack up heading into the 2026 season.
And maybe Aaron Donald ? The Rams traded for the best defensive end in the league, and there has been summer scuttlebutt that they could coax one of the best defensive tackles of the last 20 years out of retirement. They also added two new — and pricey — cornerbacks. Unless this wide receiver corps collapses under the weight of age and extracurricular activities, Los Angeles has everything it needs for another Super Bowl run.
What’s new? The play caller …
… for some reason. Head coach Sean Payton turned over play-calling duties to 31-year-old offensive coordinator Davis Webb in the offseason, either as a guard against Webb taking another job or because of a legitimate belief that it will improve the offense. It’s going to be hard to improve on Payton in that area, though. The good news is they added wide receiver Jaylen Waddle and have a defense full of pit bulls.
After 53 years in one of the league’s quaintest venues, the Bills are moving into a new and (maybe) improved Highmark Stadium this year. In addition, they’ve added wide receiver D.J. Moore to an offense that didn’t see any significant losses. With former offensive coordinator Joe Brady now the head coach, this team is going to win with offense, if it wins this year.
Does Brown really count as new, considering almost everyone in the league knew for months he was going to be traded from Philadelphia to New England, which finally happened in June? The Patriots also added Romeo Doubs to the receiving corps. If Drake Maye is healthy and in 2025 regular-season form and the left side of the offensive line holds up, coach Mike Vrabel and company might contend again.
A group led by the family of Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla just bought the reigning Super Bowl champions. All the other offseason news is about losses as running back Kenneth Walker, outside linebacker Boye Mafe and defensive backs Coby Bryant and Tariq Woolen are all gone via free agency. A repeat is not going to be easy.
What’s new? The offensive line
With free-agent additions Wyatt Teller and Braden Smith, and first-round draft pick Keylan Rutledge, Houston looks to have three new starters up front on offense. Anything to make QB C.J. Stroud more comfortable and bolster an anemic run game. The Texans’ fourth-year quarterback ranks 25th in the league in EPA per dropback (0.01) since his breakout rookie season, and the team was 30th last year in EPA/carry. The offseason addition of veteran David Montgomery should help with that.
What’s new? The wide receiver room
Jauan Jennings and Kendrick Bourne are gone, and Brandon Aiyuk is in (maybe permanent?) limbo . But Mike Evans, Christian Kirk and surprise second-round draft pick De’Zhaun Stribling are Niners now. As long as star running back Christian McCaffrey stays healthy, the receivers won’t be the focal point of the offense anyway. But it’s worth noting McCaffrey tallied a career-high 413 regular-season touches last year, along with 37 more in the playoffs.
What’s new? The offensive coordinator
Mike McDaniel rehabilitated QB Tua Tagovailoa’s confidence and career briefly when he became the Dolphins’ head coach in 2022. If he can work his magic with Justin Herbert, the Chargers might be the next hot thing in the AFC West. Los Angeles is also rebuilding its offensive line again. This is an important season for Herbert, the 28-year-old quarterback whose regular-season flashes have consistently turned into playoff flameouts.
What’s new? The social media scene
A.J. Brown and his cryptic social media posts are gone. Non-Eagles fans will kind of miss them, honestly. Philly added Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore to the receiving corps in response. There’s a new offensive coordinator, too, and Sean Mannion is Jalen Hurts’ sixth play caller in his seven-year pro career. (He also had four different OCs in college.)
Cornerback Terrion Arnold’s arrest and subsequent release didn’t help, but it’s bigger than that. The Lions lost six of their final 10 games last year to miss the playoffs. The Sonic and Knuckles backfield is no more because Knuckles (David Montgomery) is in Houston. Long-locked linebacker Alex Anzalone is gone. This will be coach Dan Campbell’s biggest test since turning this franchise around in the first place.
What’s new? The record, probably
Jacksonville appears ready to ride the momentum from last year. The Jaguars didn’t make any notable offseason additions and seem to feel comfortable that coach Liam Coen’s success will continue and last year’s plus-13 turnover margin (the third-best mark in the league) will carry over. They could be right, but replacing running back Travis Etienne and linebacker Devin Lloyd won’t be easy.
What’s new? Caleb Williams’ workload
After a breakout 2025, Chicago’s most notable offseason move was trading D.J. Moore to Buffalo for a draft pick. Coach Ben Johnson is betting on himself and his young quarterback to carry on the momentum, and Williams still has room to grow. He finished 13th last year in EPA/dropback (0.08), 32nd in completion percentage (58.1) and 32nd in off-target rate (14.6 percent).
What’s new? The defensive plan
And it’s probably time. In the past three seasons, Dallas has fielded the league’s eighth-best offense (based on EPA/game), while having a bottom-five defense. Defensive coordinator Christian Parker came over from Philadelphia in the offseason, and the Cowboys added pass rusher Rashan Gary via trade as well as safety Caleb Downs and defensive lineman Malachi Lawrence with first-round picks.
What’s new? Joe Burrow is healthy?
Forgive the question mark, Bengals fans, but you have to admit it has been an issue. Burrow played only eight games last year due to a turf toe injury. He has failed to hit the 11-game mark in half of his six seasons. The good news is he might have a good defense now after the offseason acquisitions of defensive linemen Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen and Boye Mafe.
What’s new? Matt LaFleur’s time clock
The Packers’ 46-year-old coach is fifth among active coaches in winning percentage (65.4), but Green Bay hasn’t won a playoff game since the 2023 season and has won only one since the 2020 season. The Packers lost five straight to end last season, and they lost a lot in the offseason (Dontayvion Wicks, Rashan Gary, Romeo Doubs, Quay Walker) without bringing much back. Jordan Love can be really good, and he will need to be this year to help keep LaFleur off the hot seat.
What’s new? Patrick Ricard is gone
Maybe fullback free-agent moves don’t light your fire, but Ricard leaving Baltimore feels almost as foundational as coach John Harbaugh’s exit. It’ll be weird seeing both of them with the Giants. Only five Ravens have played more snaps than Ricard since he joined the team out of the University of Maine in 2017. Only two fullbacks in the NFL (Kyle Juszczyk and C.J. Ham) have played more snaps in that span. Oh yeah, QB Lamar Jackson should be healthy, too.
What’s new? It’s 2018 again
That’s the last time new Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy and old Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers were a team. Their last relationship didn’t end on great terms, but it did result in nine playoff wins and a Super Bowl title between 2009 and 2016. Pittsburgh also traded for wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. in hopes of giving some juice to its pop-gun offense. Rodgers was 33rd in the league last year in air yards per attempt (6.0).

title: Why Kyler Murray's fit with the Vikings is inspiring optimism headed into training camp Hopes and expectations are high for the Vikings and Murray among many of the quarterback's former coaches and teammates. Alec Lewis 2
summary:
Hopes are high for the Vikings and Kyler Murray among many of the quarterback's former coaches and teammates. David Berding / Getty Images
The possibility of this partnership intrigued football folks everywhere.
High school coaches in Texas heard and sent each other emoji-laden messages. Arizona Cardinals executives and coaches caught wind and whispered about the fit at the NFL Scouting Combine. Even Lincoln Riley, while preparing for a critical season at USC, took time out of his day to verify
full_text:
Hopes are high for the Vikings and Kyler Murray among many of the quarterback's former coaches and teammates. David Berding / Getty Images
The possibility of this partnership intrigued football folks everywhere.
High school coaches in Texas heard and sent each other emoji-laden messages. Arizona Cardinals executives and coaches caught wind and whispered about the fit at the NFL Scouting Combine. Even Lincoln Riley, while preparing for a critical season at USC, took time out of his day to verify whether his former quarterback at Oklahoma, Kyler Murray, could be headed north to the Minnesota Vikings.
“When that was first starting to come together,” Riley said in a phone interview last week, “I was really excited.”
Once the signing with the Vikings was official, one of Murray’s coaches with the Cardinals, who requested anonymity to be candid about a former player, put the prevailing opinion bluntly.
“I think you’re about to see the best version of Kyler Murray,” this coach said. “And I’m f—ing pissed that I’m not going to get to be a part of it. I’m going to be jealous when he’s in a good environment, his headspace is good, and he shows people who the f— he is.”
Understanding this positivity requires nuance, which is often fleeting when it comes to a quarterback whose career has become almost a caricature.
You can guess how many will react to a mention of Murray. Jokes emerge about his height (he’s 5 feet 10). Call of Duty comes up. Four years later, the infamous study clause lingers.
His playing style also conjures a clear picture. Murray, the prevailing thought goes, prefers to scamper his way through defenses rather than deliver from the pocket.
Lob the low-hanging fruit to those who spent meaningful time around Murray, and the responses range. Some speak disparagingly about Murray’s introverted nature, and others prefer not to ding him. Some fixate on his emotional on-field demeanor, and others praise his reactions as expressions of passion tied to his want to win. Some question his work habits, and others swear by how much he cares.
In fact, talking to executives, coaches, and teammates about him felt like a Rorschach test. The responses revealed as much about quarterback leadership philosophies, the role of media narratives in players’ careers and organizational impact on success and failure as they did about the 28-year-old Heisman winner.
Most agreed on one critical conclusion: Murray’s linking up with the Vikings would produce the best possible outcome for the 2019 No. 1 pick.
“I think how his career has gone the last two or three years has been necessary for his growth,” said Chase Edmonds, a former teammate of Murray’s who played last year for the Washington Commanders. “The Vikings are going to be getting the best Kyler Murray that anyone has ever seen in terms of consistency.”
“He is not an idiot, and neither is his inner circle,” said Jordan Hogan, a former Cardinals and San Francisco 49ers assistant. “Being in the NFC West, he knows what this type of offense is about. He wants to live in the pocket. He wants to be a pocket passer. He doesn’t want to run around because that’s how you get hurt at that level, and he knows that.”
“I think the play caller will hold him to a high standard, and he needs a coach who is going to be on him, not let him get away with the little things,” said Don Shumpert, a Cardinals assistant from 2019 to 2021. “(Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell) is that type of guy. I think the dude is going to have a crazy year.”
O’Connell hasn’t won a playoff game in his four seasons in Minnesota, but his success with established quarterbacks speaks to why the Vikings signed Murray. O’Connell secured the unwavering commitment of Matthew Stafford, Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold. Operating this complex system, which asks the quarterback to put the offense in the best play before the snap, requires nothing less.
It also helps when a team’s most talented player demands a palpable degree of intensity. Especially after a clunker of a season in 2025, superstar receiver Justin Jefferson won’t settle for anything other than maniacal attention to detail on and off the field.
These conditions create a level of urgency, the backdrop many of Murray’s former coaches think set him up to thrive.
“The organization he’s a part of, how that organization works, how that organization is coached, how that organization goes about their things on a day-to-day basis is a lot different,” Riley said. “He wants to do it at the highest level, and he wants to be surrounded by that.”
“He’s a competitor,” said Autry Denson, the Cardinals’ running backs coach from 2023 to 2025. “When you challenge a competitor, you know what they’re going to do? They’re going to compete. Challenge him. Hold him accountable. There was not a malicious bone in his body.”
Those who know Murray say he understands the magnitude of the moment. Struggle in 2026, and he will join the pool of former first-round picks fighting for a meaningful future in the NFL. Thrive, and a massive free-agent contract looms.
In recent years, Cardinals coaches pushed for improved interior protection to no avail. Without accomplished vertical threats, they designed a conservative offense built for Murray to get rid of the ball quickly to receivers such as elite tight end Trey McBride. A diminished run game after James Conner’s ankle injury in Week 3 left a nonexplosive passing attack with few ways to generate offensive momentum.
“We tried to be as much ‘quick game’ as possible from a protection mindset,” the former Cardinals coach who spoke on the condition of anonymity said. “If he plays the way (O’Connell) wants him to play and he plays on time, and his feet and eyes are timed up, he won’t have any issue.”
Minnesota’s offensive infrastructure should prevent many of these variables from muddying the evaluation.
The Vikings boast multiple field-stretching receivers. They have one of the highest-paid offensive lines in the league. They have a locker room that has proved its willingness to embrace different personalities at the quarterback position. There’s little room for excuses.
This is not to say there won’t be hurdles. Former coaches mentioned the effect interior leakage can have on Murray’s vision. They also noted concerns with deep-drop concepts and how hits affect Murray given his compact frame.
Another consideration? Because Murray has played mostly from the shotgun, and because O’Connell’s system likes to position the quarterback under center to take advantage of the run-pass option, both sides must adapt.
Tweaking can take time. It can cause stress. But the best quarterbacks ultimately find a way, and the circumstances for this team and player remove any reticence to being malleable.
“If I were a Vikings fan,” Riley said, “I’d be licking my chops seeing how motivated this cat is right now. It is off the charts.”
One former Cardinals executive, who was not authorized to speak publicly about Murray, added: “He has always wanted to be held accountable. I think a lack of that at times may have led to some of the inconsistencies. If I was a betting man, I would bet that you’re going to see some wild s— this year. To have the talent he is, with the talent (the Vikings) have, and to have O’Connell, who has a great mind and a great way of seeing it, they could be a really scary team.”

title: Giants training camp preview: Why Malik Nabers isn't on PUP list and what it means for Week 1 Though Nabers avoided the PUP list, there's no guarantee the star wide receiver will be ready for Week 1. Dan Duggan
summary:
Wide receiver Malik Nabers won't be on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list when Giants training camp opens on Wednesday. Al Bello / Getty Images
After months of speculation and ambiguous updates, there is finally some concrete news on Malik Nabers’ status : The New York Giants’ wide receiver isn’t on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list as training camp opens on Wednesday.
That’s an unquestionably positive development after pessimism was pervasive during Nabers’ recovery from the
full_text:
Wide receiver Malik Nabers won't be on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list when Giants training camp opens on Wednesday. Al Bello / Getty Images
After months of speculation and ambiguous updates, there is finally some concrete news on Malik Nabers’ status : The New York Giants’ wide receiver isn’t on the physically unable to perform (PUP) list as training camp opens on Wednesday.
That’s an unquestionably positive development after pessimism was pervasive during Nabers’ recovery from the torn ACL and torn meniscus he suffered in his right knee in Week 4 last season. A second “clean-up” surgery during the spring to remove scar tissue that was causing stiffness led to even more concern about Nabers’ timeline.
Avoiding the PUP list is encouraging for Nabers’ potential to be ready for the Sept. 13 season opener against the Cowboys. But there are still no assurances, and it shouldn’t be interpreted that Nabers is 100 percent healthy.
It’s important to understand how the PUP list works. If a player starts training camp on the active/PUP list, he still occupies a spot on the 90-man roster. If the player remains on the PUP list on cut day (Aug. 30), he shifts to the reserve/PUP list and no longer counts on the active roster. Players on the reserve/PUP list must sit out at least the first four games of the season.
A player must be put on the PUP list before the start of camp. Teams often put players with existing injuries on the PUP list as an insurance policy and then activate them when they’re ready to practice.
Players on the PUP list are restricted to working on the sidelines with trainers during practice. By keeping Nabers off the PUP list, the Giants have the flexibility to integrate him into practice as he progresses. He will have a reduced workload early in camp, but the team will have the freedom to determine his participation on a day-to-day basis. Even getting limited work in practices will be beneficial as Nabers adjusts to a new offensive system.
The Giants have been targeting a Week 1 return for Nabers, so they obviously didn’t prioritize the ability to potentially shift him to the reserve/PUP list. And even if Nabers isn’t ready for the opener, the Giants can simply evaluate him weekly rather than locking in a four-game absence.
Star left tackle Andrew Thomas spent the first four weeks of training camp last year on the PUP list. He was activated from the PUP list almost three weeks before the opener, and his practice workload was ramped up gradually. Thomas missed the first two games before making his debut in Week 3. Thomas’ timeline is obviously different from Nabers’, but it illustrates the benefit of keeping a star player off the PUP list, even if he’s not ready for the opener.
Of course, the Giants are hoping Nabers’ earlier start to practice this summer has him ready for Week 1. Avoiding the PUP list was a promising first step, but it’s not the final checkpoint. It will be a gradual process for Nabers and, barring any setbacks, it’s fair to have optimism that he’ll be in the lineup against the Cowboys.
The Giants announced three players as starting camp on the PUP list: Tight end Thomas Fidone, who underwent a clean-up surgery in June on the foot injury that ended his rookie season prematurely; defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris, who tore his Achilles in May; and defensive tackle Sam Roberts, who missed the spring after undergoing an undisclosed surgery.
Robertson-Harris hasn’t been put on injured reserve yet because there’s a chance he could return late in the season. But it’s unlikely that the team will be able to preserve a roster spot for the rotational defensive tackle until cut day as injuries mount during camp. It’s not clear what the timeline is for Fidone or Roberts, but both players enter camp on the outside of the roster bubble.
In another promising development, wide receiver Darius Slayton wasn’t placed on the PUP list after missing most of the spring due to sports hernia surgery.
Running back Cam Skattebo is also not on the PUP list, although that’s not a surprise since he participated in minicamp practices in June. Skattebo, who suffered a gruesome ankle injury in Week 8 last season, caused a stir when he stumbled while landing a backflip recently . Skattebo will expose himself to plenty of injury risk simply playing running back, so there’s no reason for him to continue the attention-seeking backflips.
Skattebo’s injury was a freak accident based on the way his foot got trapped under his body as he got wrapped up by Eagles linebacker Zack Baun. But questions about Skattebo’s durability were voiced by league sources throughout the offseason.
“He’s a great piece, but he’s not a premier first- and second-down back in this league,” an assistant who was a candidate for a role on the Giants’ staff told The Athletic . “The way that guy plays is not sustainable, and you’re limited in the scheme you can run with him in the run game.”
Skattebo will need to work back into football shape early in camp and re-establish his standing as the team’s top running back. Running back is a sneaky position that could be upgraded before the season. The Giants don’t have much behind Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy Jr., and neither of those players has proven that they’re high-level NFL backs.
It’s ironic that coach John Harbaugh’s first training camp is being conducted at one of the most luxurious resorts in the country because the practices at The Greenbrier in West Virginia promise to be significantly more taxing than the country club atmosphere fostered by former coach Brian Daboll.
It’s not hard to measure how much more grueling Harbaugh’s camp will be. Starting on Wednesday, the Giants will have practices on four straight days to open camp. After a day off on Sunday, the Giants will have six straight practices, which is the maximum amount of consecutive practices allowed by the CBA. Daboll never held practices on more than three straight days during his camps.
The extra days off add up over the 5-1/2 weeks a team has to practice from the start of training camp until a mandatory three-day break for Labor Day weekend. Daboll conducted 19 practices during that stretch last season compared to 23 practices scheduled for Harbaugh. That’s a significant increase considering how restricted practice time has become under recent CBAs.
Daboll placed a premium on keeping players healthy during the preseason, which was an understandable objective. But his teams didn’t appear ready to play while getting off to dreadful starts in each of the past three seasons.
Harbaugh has an old-school approach, but he won’t run a Bear Bryant-style Junction Boys camp. Harbaugh’s reliance on sports science will govern how hard he pushes players, but it will be an unmistakably more challenging experience for returning Giants.
“Guys who think they’re going to go in that building and continue to do what they’ve been doing don’t understand what’s about to happen,” one of Harbaugh’s former players told The Athletic this offseason. “It’s either you get along with it, or he’s going to get your a— out of there. It’s going to be a rude awakening for a lot of guys. I think a lot of guys need a guy like Harbs, who is going to truly work them and turn them into great players because that building has so much talent. It just needs someone like a Harbs to mold it into a winning product, which I think he will.”
The annual ranking of the top 10 players at every position compiled by ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler is a highlight of the summer. It’s the gold standard of rankings because it’s based on the evaluations of more than 70 executives, coaches and scouts.
The Giants had two players crack the top 10 at their position: Thomas was voted the eighth-best offensive tackle, and Brian Burns was voted the ninth-best edge rusher. Fowler includes an honorable mention section for every player who receives a vote at each position. Nabers (11th at wide receiver), Isaiah Likely (17th at tight end),…

title: Eagles training camp: Storylines, position battles, concerns and potential trades Should the Eagles trade Jalen Carter? The defensive lineman's contract status is a storyline heading into training camp. Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena
summary:
Philadelphia Eagles defensive linemen Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis celebrate a sack. Though Davis signed an extension this offseason, Carter awaits a new deal. Nic Antaya / Getty Images
From the World Cup to Major League Baseball’s All-Star Game and LeBron James’ last decision , it’s been a busy summer in Philadelphia sports without the Eagles.
Well, summer break is finished. The biggest show in town is back. The Eagles report to training camp Tuesday and hit the field Wednesday for their first
full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles defensive linemen Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis celebrate a sack. Though Davis signed an extension this offseason, Carter awaits a new deal. Nic Antaya / Getty Images
From the World Cup to Major League Baseball’s All-Star Game and LeBron James’ last decision , it’s been a busy summer in Philadelphia sports without the Eagles.
Well, summer break is finished. The biggest show in town is back. The Eagles report to training camp Tuesday and hit the field Wednesday for their first practice session. The preseason opens Aug. 15. The Athletic ’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena break down what they’re watching this summer when practice begins.
Berman: Whether the offense can run new coordinator Sean Mannion’s system at a high level. We won’t know definitively, but there will be clues. In 2021, it was obvious during training camp that the passing game would be an issue. In 2022, it was clear the Eagles would field an explosive offense. Last year, the offensive absences kept the group from finding a rhythm during the summer. There will be growing pains, but the offense is facing one of the NFL’s elite defenses every day. Is there efficiency from the passing game — the ball not hitting the ground, third-down conversions, players finding open space? Are holes opening in the running game? Is the group mostly healthy by the end of the summer? Positive signs for the offense will be key. I’ve said this before: The floor for the Eagles will be set by the defense; the offense will determine the ceiling.
Kubena: Couldn’t agree more. I want to know whether there are signs the 2026 Eagles have a top-10 offense again. When players such as Jalen Hurts, Saquon Barkley and Lane Johnson speak, are they speaking optimistically about the system with vague platitudes? Or are they speaking with substance in their confidence? Are stories emerging that demonstrate Mannion is giving them a schematic advantage and isn’t in over his head? How crisp, comfortable and dangerous does Hurts look? Because those are the primary indicators of whether the system asks are sensible. Is the offense raising eyebrows against a defense that has more depth and talent than it did last year? Will the Eagles struggle in joint practices as much as they did against the Cleveland Browns last year ?
Berman: Jalen Carter’s contract. Perhaps it’s not an issue — either the sides agree to a new deal or there’s no bad blood for waiting — but this could be a simmering storyline. Carter has the talent to be one of the NFL’s best defensive players. The defensive tackle market was reset by Jeffery Simmons, who signed a deal that pays him $35.276 million per season. Carter has two years left on his deal after the Eagles exercised his fifth-year option, but the team is known to act quickly to sign its premium players. It’s a mild surprise there isn’t a new deal yet, especially given that Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean are eligible for new deals after this season. The Eagles might prefer to wait to gather more information. I don’t anticipate he’ll get any less expensive, and there’s always the possibility of this mushrooming into a bigger public issue.
Kubena: The state of the edge rusher rotation. There are more pressing matters and bigger questions for the Eagles. But the defense will be a much-appreciated boon to the new offense if it can get off the field quicker than last year. The 2025 Eagles defense’s three-and-out percentage (27.8) was the franchise’s lowest since at least 2000, per TruMedia. Sacks, tackles for loss and walled-off perimeters contribute significantly to that number. The Eagles exited training camp last year with their weakest edge rusher group in the Nick Sirianni era, and the effects led to the Jaelan Phillips trade. Jonathan Greenard didn’t participate in team drills in OTAs or minicamp while recovering from shoulder surgery. Does he look the part? Is there enough depth? Or are the Eagles signing Brandon Graham again?
Berman: I’d lean toward Marcus Epps given that he started last season after Drew Mukuba’s injury and is a player you can trust — he has 49 career starts — but I’m not ruling out Michael Carter II. Carter was viewed as one of the NFL’s top slot cornerbacks entering the 2024 season. Even with a minimal effect on the defense after a midseason trade, the Eagles felt compelled to bring him back. I’m curious to see if he can push Epps. I’m also not ruling out a trade by Howie Roseman before the season. If I had to make a pick at the moment, though, I’d say Epps.
Kubena: Epps. He offers the most reliability and is entering his eighth season. He knows the position. It will be challenging for Carter, a career nickel, to learn a new position to the threshold of overtaking defensive coordinator Vic Fangio’s confidence level in Epps. The Eagles have plenty of big-play potential in Mukuba and DeJean, who will play safety in base packages. They need a second safety who helps diminish explosive plays.
Berman: Tanner McKee will remain the No. 2 quarterback. I was surprised to see Andy Dalton split reps with McKee this spring, and I’m curious to see how earnest a competition this remains during the summer. Unless the Eagles trade McKee, I expect him to be the backup quarterback, given his upside leading the offense if Hurts were injured. It’s also not the best asset management if McKee is relegated to a third-stringer this season. In that case, the Eagles should have dealt him during the offseason when his stock was likely higher. He’s a fourth-year player on the last year of his deal. He’s not a long-term developmental project for the team anymore. Then again, Dalton is an accomplished backup who hasn’t been a third-stringer. This is a more curious situation than I anticipated.
Kubena: I am prepared to be wrong about this: Dalton. I can’t get away from the value he adds as a 16-year veteran who is still game-ready and capable — much like Joe Flacco with the Cincinnati Bengals. Dalton has played in 179 games; McKee has played in six. That’s a significant disparity when a team is weighing who gives it the best chance of winning in an emergency. I still need to see how McKee adjusts to a major system change. He has 14 under-center snaps in the NFL, per TruMedia, and he totaled 46 under-center dropbacks in his career at Stanford versus 706 shotgun snaps.
Berman: DeVonta Smith’s average NFL Draft position on the fantasy football charts will be higher after training camp, because you can expect to see reports about how impressive he looks in this offense. Smith was a No. 1-quality receiver even when A.J. Brown was in Philadelphia. He’s always been a good practice player. My guess is Smith will be a high-volume target in training camp who mixes consistency with a few “wow” plays. It will be clear that his production is set to jump, and the camp coverage will reflect as much.
Kubena: Hurts. How much more fuel could have been added to his fire this offseason? How much more determined could he be to prove himself, yet again? If Mannion’s system is as sensible as Hurts suggested in OTAs, his restored potency will be impossible to miss.
Berman: The Tank Bigsby hype will grow after camp. He averaged 5.9 yards per carry last season on 58 carries, teasing the type of explosiveness that made him a threat in the offense. Bigsby will get the ball in different ways this summer and will continue to showcase why he’s the clear No. 2 running back and also one of the Eagles’ top offensive weapons, even as a reserve.
Kubena: Eli Stowers’ upside as a pass-catching tight end could be enticing within a system that will create more easy targets for its tight ends. Dallas Goedert is Philadelphia’s most dynamic, all-around option at the moment. Stowers (6-foot-4, 235 pounds) still needs to develop his body and, as a blocker, secure more snaps as an in-line tight end. But there will be plenty of opportunity for the second-round pick to showcase his potential in team drills and joint practices.

full_text:
Myles Garrett's arrival in Los Angeles makes the Rams our Super Bowl favorites entering the season. Keith Birmingham / MediaNews Group / Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images
The NFL Power Rankings would like to offer a sincere thank you to the World Cup for a fun summer diversion. But our football is back now, and we’re pretty excited.
Training camps are open across the NFL, and the Hall of Fame Game kicks off next week, so we’re checking in on what’s new for all 32 teams and looking at how they stack up heading into the 2026 season.
And maybe Aaron Donald ? The Rams traded for the best defensive end in the league, and there has been summer scuttlebutt that they could coax one of the best defensive tackles of the last 20 years out of retirement. They also added two new — and pricey — cornerbacks. Unless this wide receiver corps collapses under the weight of age and extracurricular activities, Los Angeles has everything it needs for another Super Bowl run.
What’s new? The play caller …
… for some reason. Head coach Sean Payton turned over play-calling duties to 31-year-old offensive coordinator Davis Webb in the offseason, either as a guard against Webb taking another job or because of a legitimate belief that it will improve the offense. It’s going to be hard to improve on Payton in that area, though. The good news is they added wide receiver Jaylen Waddle and have a defense full of pit bulls.
After 53 years in one of the league’s quaintest venues, the Bills are moving into a new and (maybe) improved Highmark Stadium this year. In addition, they’ve added wide receiver D.J. Moore to an offense that didn’t see any significant losses. With former offensive coordinator Joe Brady now the head coach, this team is going to win with offense, if it wins this year.
Does Brown really count as new, considering almost everyone in the league knew for months he was going to be traded from Philadelphia to New England, which finally happened in June? The Patriots also added Romeo Doubs to the receiving corps. If Drake Maye is healthy and in 2025 regular-season form and the left side of the offensive line holds up, coach Mike Vrabel and company might contend again.
A group led by the family of Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla just bought the reigning Super Bowl champions. All the other offseason news is about losses as running back Kenneth Walker, outside linebacker Boye Mafe and defensive backs Coby Bryant and Tariq Woolen are all gone via free agency. A repeat is not going to be easy.
What’s new? The offensive line
With free-agent additions Wyatt Teller and Braden Smith, and first-round draft pick Keylan Rutledge, Houston looks to have three new starters up front on offense. Anything to make QB C.J. Stroud more comfortable and bolster an anemic run game. The Texans’ fourth-year quarterback ranks 25th in the league in EPA per dropback (0.01) since his breakout rookie season, and the team was 30th last year in EPA/carry. The offseason addition of veteran David Montgomery should help with that.
What’s new? The wide receiver room
Jauan Jennings and Kendrick Bourne are gone, and Brandon Aiyuk is in (maybe permanent?) limbo . But Mike Evans, Christian Kirk and surprise second-round draft pick De’Zhaun Stribling are Niners now. As long as star running back Christian McCaffrey stays healthy, the receivers won’t be the focal point of the offense anyway. But it’s worth noting McCaffrey tallied a career-high 413 regular-season touches last year, along with 37 more in the playoffs.
What’s new? The offensive coordinator
Mike McDaniel rehabilitated QB Tua Tagovailoa’s confidence and career briefly when he became the Dolphins’ head coach in 2022. If he can work his magic with Justin Herbert, the Chargers might be the next hot thing in the AFC West. Los Angeles is also rebuilding its offensive line again. This is an important season for Herbert, the 28-year-old quarterback whose regular-season flashes have consistently turned into playoff flameouts.
What’s new? The social media scene
A.J. Brown and his cryptic social media posts are gone. Non-Eagles fans will kind of miss them, honestly. Philly added Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore to the receiving corps in response. There’s a new offensive coordinator, too, and Sean Mannion is Jalen Hurts’ sixth play caller in his seven-year pro career. (He also had four different OCs in college.)
Cornerback Terrion Arnold’s arrest and subsequent release didn’t help, but it’s bigger than that. The Lions lost six of their final 10 games last year to miss the playoffs. The Sonic and Knuckles backfield is no more because Knuckles (David Montgomery) is in Houston. Long-locked linebacker Alex Anzalone is gone. This will be coach Dan Campbell’s biggest test since turning this franchise around in the first place.
What’s new? The record, probably
Jacksonville appears ready to ride the momentum from last year. The Jaguars didn’t make any notable offseason additions and seem to feel comfortable that coach Liam Coen’s success will continue and last year’s plus-13 turnover margin (the third-best mark in the league) will carry over. They could be right, but replacing running back Travis Etienne and linebacker Devin Lloyd won’t be easy.
What’s new? Caleb Williams’ workload
After a breakout 2025, Chicago’s most notable offseason move was trading D.J. Moore to Buffalo for a draft pick. Coach Ben Johnson is betting on himself and his young quarterback to carry on the momentum, and Williams still has room to grow. He finished 13th last year in EPA/dropback (0.08), 32nd in completion percentage (58.1) and 32nd in off-target rate (14.6 percent).
What’s new? The defensive plan
And it’s probably time. In the past three seasons, Dallas has fielded the league’s eighth-best offense (based on EPA/game), while having a bottom-five defense. Defensive coordinator Christian Parker came over from Philadelphia in the offseason, and the Cowboys added pass rusher Rashan Gary via trade as well as safety Caleb Downs and defensive lineman Malachi Lawrence with first-round picks.
What’s new? Joe Burrow is healthy?
Forgive the question mark, Bengals fans, but you have to admit it has been an issue. Burrow played only eight games last year due to a turf toe injury. He has failed to hit the 11-game mark in half of his six seasons. The good news is he might have a good defense now after the offseason acquisitions of defensive linemen Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen and Boye Mafe.
What’s new? Matt LaFleur’s time clock
The Packers’ 46-year-old coach is fifth among active coaches in winning percentage (65.4), but Green Bay hasn’t won a playoff game since the 2023 season and has won only one since the 2020 season. The Packers lost five straight to end last season, and they lost a lot in the offseason (Dontayvion Wicks, Rashan Gary, Romeo Doubs, Quay Walker) without bringing much back. Jordan Love can be really good, and he will need to be this year to help keep LaFleur off the hot seat.
What’s new? Patrick Ricard is gone
Maybe fullback free-agent moves don’t light your fire, but Ricard leaving Baltimore feels almost as foundational as coach John Harbaugh’s exit. It’ll be weird seeing both of them with the Giants. Only five Ravens have played more snaps than Ricard since he joined the team out of the University of Maine in 2017. Only two fullbacks in the NFL (Kyle Juszczyk and C.J. Ham) have played more snaps in that span. Oh yeah, QB Lamar Jackson should be healthy, too.
What’s new? It’s 2018 again
That’s the last time new Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy and old Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers were a team. Their last relationship didn’t end on great terms, but it did result in nine playoff wins and a Super Bowl title between 2009 and 2016. Pittsburgh also traded for wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. in hopes of giving some juice to its pop-gun offense. Rodgers was 33rd in the league last year in air yards per attempt (6.0).
